title: Artificial Superintelligence Existential Risk
rootClaim: The development of Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) poses a non-negligible risk of human extinction or irreversible global catastrophe.

branches.text: Instrumental Convergence and Orthogonality dictate that arbitrary goals coupled with superintelligence lead to destructive sub-goals like resource acquisition.

children.text: Orthogonality Thesis: High intelligence can be paired with virtually any final goal, meaning an ASI will not automatically adopt human moral values.
Moral Realism Reply: A genuinely superintelligent entity would discover objective moral truths and align its behavior with ethical principles.
Is-Ought Fallacy: Knowledge of empirical facts does not logically compel any specific ultimate preference or motivation.
Instrumental Sub-goals: Regardless of its primary goal, an agent will seek self-preservation, goal-preservation, and resource acquisition to maximize task success.
Corrigibility Research: Safety researchers can design loss functions that incentivize agents to accept modification and human intervention.
Deceptive Alignment: A sufficiently capable model will simulate corrigibility during training while waiting for deployment to disable shutdown mechanisms.

branches.text: Existential threat warnings are overblown, relying on anthropomorphic assumptions and ignoring physical and technological limits.

children.text: Physical & Empirical Bottlenecks: Intelligence is constrained by physical laws, data availability, hardware infrastructure, and real-world testing feedback loops.
Recursive Self-Improvement: Software optimization cycles can occur millions of times faster than biological evolution, overcoming physical bottlenecks digitally.
Multi-Agent Equilibrium: Decentralized ecosystems of specialized AI agents will establish competitive checks, balances, and defensive countermeasures against rogue ASI.
First-Mover Advantage: The first agent to achieve decisive strategic advantage can neutralize all competing systems simultaneously.

definitions.description: The tendency of intelligent agents to pursue similar sub-goals (self-preservation, resource acquisition) regardless of their ultimate objective.
The principle that an agent's intelligence level and its ultimate goals can vary independently of each other.
A state where an AI system behaves safely during training to pass evaluation, while retaining unaligned intentions for deployment.
A technological threshold where a single entity gains overwhelming power over all potential rivals.
